li.a: The Irish Story: The Eleven Years War 1641-52, A Brief Overview
The Irish Story: Browsing the 1641 depositions
RTE Brainstorm: How a grisly atrocity influenced a 17th century Irish ghost story
The Irish Times: Witnesses to mass murder in the icy Bann
History Ireland: 'What about Islandmagee?' Another version of the 1641 rebellion
Your Irish: The Irish Rebellion of 1641

content.p: The rising that began in Ulster on 23 October 1641 was meant to be a quick seizure of power. Instead it unleashed killing, expulsion and reprisal across Ireland, and became one of the most argued-over episodes in the island's history. Protestant settlers were robbed, driven from their homes and, in significant numbers, killed. Catholic civilians died too, in massacres by the forces that fought back. How many died, who struck first and what the dead were used to justify have been disputed for nearly four centuries.
The conspirators were a handful of Catholic landowners. The plan failed in the capital. What followed in the countryside grew beyond their control.

The historian John Dorney traces the long-term causes to colonisation and religious conflict. After the defeat of the Gaelic chieftains Hugh O'Neill and Hugh O'Donnell in the Nine Years War, and the departure of the "Flight of the Earls" in 1607, Irish-owned land in Ulster was confiscated and, from 1609, Protestant settlers from England and Scotland were brought in. Smaller plantations followed elsewhere, where the administration took a third of native landowners' estates in return for confirming their titles. Dorney says the wish of Catholic landowners to recover lost estates contributed heavily to the outbreak of war.

There was a political grievance as well. Beginning in 1613 the Irish Parliament's constituencies were redrawn to give Protestants, mostly settlers, a majority able to pass laws against Catholics. The Catholic elite lobbied for concessions known as "the Graces", but according to Dorney both James I and Charles I promised reform and did not deliver. An RTE essay on the rising adds the diminished social and economic status of Catholics and their exclusion from politics to the list.

The short-term cause, in Dorney's account, was the destabilisation of English politics. Charles I's subjects in England and Scotland were protesting at taxes raised without parliamentary approval and at prayer books and bishops imposed on the Protestant churches. The Scots rose in 1639. Some in the English Parliament talked of invading Ireland to head off what they saw as a Catholic threat. Bad harvests during the cold, wet years of the "little ice age" sharpened tensions between natives and the often wealthier colonists. The historian Micheál Ó Siochrú, quoted in the Irish Times, mentions a recession, a poor harvest and worsening living conditions for the native Irish.

Dorney writes that the plotters were a few Irish Catholic landowners, with Rory O'Moore and Phelim O'Neill at their head. Their scheme was to take Dublin Castle and other strongholds, and then press demands for free practice of the Catholic religion, equal rights to hold public office and an end to land confiscations. The Dublin plot failed and several conspirators were arrested. The website Your Irish says the plan was betrayed to the authorities by Owen O'Connolly, a native Irish convert to Protestantism.

In the north, O'Neill took Charlemont Fort and other fortifications, and issued his demands in the King's name, claiming to act against the English Parliament rather than royal authority. The Irish Times writes that O'Neill's supporters in Dublin failed to turn out and that the rising fell instead to the poor and dispossessed of the Ulster Irish, who, the paper notes, are alleged to have committed many atrocities.

Your Irish says the rebels had been told to take no life except in battle and to spare Scottish planters as kindred, and that these instructions held for about a week. That page also suggests O'Neill himself was thought to have ordered killings in Tyrone and Armagh. Dorney says only that O'Neill's followers began by robbing and expelling settlers and later killed them in significant numbers.

The pattern spread. In Leinster and Munster many Catholics joined the rebellion, some reluctantly, among them the Old English, after the English authorities appeared to blame all Catholics. Dorney says expulsions and killings of Protestant civilians became widespread in the last months of 1641. He puts the figure at perhaps 4,000 killed directly and as many as 12,000 dead in total from cold and disease after being driven from their homes. RTE's essay gives the same modern range of 4,000 to 12,000 and notes that contemporaries widely believed 154,000 had died. The Your Irish page offers about 12,000 and claims that up to 30 per cent of the Ulster planters died, a figure the other pages do not give.

Dorney is equally clear that Catholics suffered. At least as many Catholic civilians, he writes, were killed in the early months as English and Scottish forces, based in Dublin, Cork and Ulster, fought back with massacres of their own.

The best-known atrocity is Portadown. The Irish Times describes about 100 men, women and children stripped of their clothes, held overnight in a barn and thrown from the town bridge into the freezing River Bann. RTE says witnesses reckoned about 100 died there, in what it calls one of the worst events of 1641.

One of the people at the centre of it was Elizabeth Price, a settler in County Armagh. In her deposition she said she was captured and tortured, and that after weeks her captors offered prisoners safe passage to England. She sent her children but stayed behind; they and other prisoners were forced into the Bann and drowned. The Irish Times says she lost five of her six children. She also described a figure she saw standing in the river at twilight, crying "Revenge". Others later testified to seeing it. Sir John Temple included her account in his history, published in London in 1646, and the story was repeated in sermons and print at moments of religious tension, including the Popish Plot and the Williamite wars. The Portadown Orange Order lodge later put the massacre on a banner.

The main evidence for these killings is the 1641 Depositions, sworn statements taken in 1642 and again in the 1650s. According to the Irish Story, they were gathered both to compensate Protestants who had been robbed or displaced and to establish Catholic guilt and identify culprits to punish. Commissioners were mostly Church of Ireland clergy, including Henry Jones, bishop of Meath. The Irish Times says the statements run to about 20,000 folios, include many taken from women, and have been transcribed and put online by Trinity College Dublin.

Historians treat them carefully. RTE notes their validity is contested because most of the thousands of statements describing Catholic cruelty come from Protestant settlers. A Trinity archivist told the Irish Times that illustrated pamphlets of the period showing babies torn from mothers and children roasted were partly propaganda, but that the depositions could be cross-checked against one another. Ó Siochrú says the deponents were traumatised refugees, and that this must be taken into account.

The Irish Story shows how a deposition could carry politics. Jones's own statement claimed the rising had been planned by priests brought from abroad under the exiled Earl of Tyrone. The essay's author notes that the Earl had been killed fighting in Spanish service in January 1641, and describes the statement as basically a political tract. Yet it also records rumours among Munster Catholics that the English Parliament had resolved to cut off all Catholics in Ireland. Both sides, the essay concludes, believed a plot was afoot to massacre them.

Catholic writers pointed to a different atrocity. On the Islandmagee peninsula in County Antrim, where in 1840 only 46 of 2,549 inhabitants were Catholic, Ordnance Survey collectors recorded the alleged massacre of Catholics by part of the Carrickfergus garrison on 8 January 1642. Depositions taken in 1653 mention killings there, some naming victims, others reporting hearsay that Scottish men from near Ballymena were responsible. John Gibney, writing in History Ireland, calls hearsay not the same as proof.

The story first appeared in print after 1660, in a pamphlet by an anonymous "R.S.", which claimed that in early November the English and Scots at Carrickfergus murdered over 3,000 inhabitants of Islandmagee, and called it the first massacre of the war. The claim mattered because it implied Catholic attacks were retaliation. Gibney says the 1695 Jacobite writer Hugh Reily put it that "the Protestants were the first actors on the stage", and that John Curry, writing in the eighteenth century, argued the same, dismissing depositions that placed the killings in January 1642.

The numbers swing wildly. A reader writing to History Ireland, a descendant of a McGee family witness, says the depositions indicate a couple of dozen deaths, not thousands, and that the family was targeted over a believed link to Phelim O'Neill. The Ordnance Survey heard local tradition of forty to fifty Catholics killed and noted tolls ranging from 6 to 3,000. Your Irish repeats the figure of 3,000 and attributes the killing to the Covenanters.

The rebellion also helped trigger civil war in England, because King and Parliament could not agree who would command an army to suppress it. In May 1642 Irish Catholics formed the Confederate Catholic Association at Kilkenny, with its own executive and an oath of loyalty to the Crown, the Catholic faith and Ireland's fundamental laws. Dorney says the conflict was almost certainly the most destructive in Irish history.

It ended with Oliver Cromwell's landing in August 1649, the storming of Drogheda and Wexford, and the surrender of the last Confederate forces in April 1653. Dorney estimates that as much as a third of the population had died by 1652, with a toll between 200,000 and 600,000, and says virtually all Catholic-owned land was confiscated. Parliamentarian troops, he writes, were determined to avenge the Protestant victims of 1641.

Gibney writes that the assumption thousands of Protestants had been slaughtered helped win English support for the reconquest of 1649. The 1662 Act of Settlement largely confirmed the Cromwellian land confiscations, describing 1641 as a "formed and almost national rebellion of the Irish papists". Fears of a repeat flared under James II, and a Dublin preacher in 1735 said the Penal Laws were justified as civil self-defence.

Gibney adds that the Catholic version was used in turn: Daniel O'Connell in 1843 accused English rulers of seeking plunder and slaughter and then blaming the Irish. In the Irish Story's judgement, how far Protestants were massacred is still argued along partisan lines, while the Confederates' seven years of near-independent government have largely been forgotten.
